source.title: Implicit Regularization in ReLU Networks with the Square Loss

record.tranche_reason: The paper gives theoretical and empirical results about implicit regularization in ReLU networks, arguing that parameter-only regularization generally cannot characterize the training dynamics; it also gives a norm bound and an assumed-condition result for a one-hidden-neuron network. These refine how implicit regularization may relate to generalization, but the paper does not measure train–test generalization gaps.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's results that bear on claim versions: the single-ReLU-neuron norm comparison and bound, the one-hidden-neuron empirical dynamics, and balancedness. The paper does not test natural-label versus random-label generalization, width scaling, image architecture comparisons, optimizer or batch-size effects, dropout, sharpness-gap correlations, or memorized-example removal. Cited prior work is not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study analyzes solution selection by gradient flow in realizable square-loss regression. Its impossibility results concern exact characterization by a data-independent parameter regularizer, not any of V1–V8. It reports neither held-out performance nor magnitude-aware sharpness, so it does not test V7 or challenge its correlational claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly right but needs narrower wording: for a single ReLU neuron, any data-independent parameter regularizer that universally characterizes zero-loss gradient-flow limits from zero must be constant on nonzero parameters. Conditional on zero-loss convergence, distance from initialization is nevertheless bounded within a factor of two of the closest zero-loss distance. For a single-hidden-ReLU network, under Assumption 6.1 and the specified infinitesimal initialization, such a regularizer must be constant on nonzero balanced parameters. This restricts exact regularizer-based descriptions; it does not prove that the dynamics have no additional bias or that networks fail to generalize.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes gradient flow on realizable square-loss ReLU regression problems and a small empirical gradient-descent simulation. The claim versions concern generalization errors on natural labels, image architectures, optimizer and batch-size comparisons, dropout, sharpness metrics, and memorized examples; these are not the same recipe or outcome.
record.method_sensitivity: For the single-neuron example, the converged parameter varies with input parameter γ. The paper's one-hidden-neuron theorem is conditional on Assumption 6.1; its empirical evidence varies γ and initialization ε.

fits_no_version.finding: The constructed single-ReLU problems share zero-loss solutions but gradient flow selects different points as input geometry changes. Theorem 4.2 then proves that a universal parameter-only regularizer must be constant away from zero.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For a single ReLU neuron in dimension at least three, square-loss gradient flow from zero cannot be characterized exactly by a nontrivial data-independent parameter regularizer.

fits_no_version.finding: Conditional on convergence to zero loss, the final distance from initialization is at most twice the distance to the closest zero-loss solution.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For a single neuron with a monotonically non-decreasing activation, convergent square-loss gradient flow controls distance from initialization within a factor of two of the minimum feasible distance.

fits_no_version.finding: Finite gradient-descent simulations support Assumption 6.1. Under that assumption, Theorem 6.2 makes any universal parameter-only regularizer constant on nonzero balanced parameters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For a single-hidden-ReLU network in dimension at least three, infinitesimal-initialization square-loss gradient flow admits no exact data-independent parameter regularizer that distinguishes nonzero balanced solutions, conditional on Assumption 6.1.

record.problems: The paper does not measure train–test error or generalization-gap outcomes. The depth-2 result depends on Assumption 6.1, motivated by finite-step gradient descent experiments for only two input settings; the paper explicitly notes that this part is empirical rather than a theoretical proof.
record.rows_left_out: No additional reported results bearing on the listed versions were omitted.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label memorization and natural-label held-out accuracy, including chance performance on random labels.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image generalization and the contributions of locality or initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects on held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout effects on held-out error across data sizes, dropout strengths and augmentation settings.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps and its ranking relative to norm- or margin-based measures.
Test-accuracy effects of removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T5 classification conflates a limitation of an implicit-regularization explanation with a test of the listed empirical claims. No version-specific verdict is warranted.

versions.untested_parts: No natural-label or random-label training/test accuracy is measured.
No width sweep or train/test error by network width is reported.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-classification comparison is performed.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparison is performed.
No sharpness or generalization-gap measure is reported.
No memorized-example removal or retraining experiment is performed.
